name: Bone microfracture for height

lead: Some teens on height forums propose that repeated impact on the legs, such as sprinting on hard surfaces or one-leg jumps, causes tiny bone fractures that the body repairs with new growth, adding height.
No published trial has tested this for height. Bone does adapt to loading in general, but length growth happens at the growth plates, which fuse after puberty.[1][2]

paras: Forum posts mention high-impact exercises such as sprinting on asphalt, single-leg jumps, push presses and squats, sometimes with ankle weights, usually by teenagers who believe their growth plates are still open.[3]
Injury to growth plates (Salter-Harris fractures) tends to interfere with growth rather than add height, and stress injuries such as shin splints or stress fractures are possible.[2]

angle.text: The idea is pursued as a no-surgery route to a few extra centimetres in adolescents. It is a community theory; the mechanism is that of general bone remodelling, not a documented route to longer bones.

lead: Bone microfracture for height is a fringe idea in height-focused looksmaxxing communities that deliberately stressing the leg bones, especially in teenagers with open growth plates, produces microscopic fractures whose repair stimulates additional growth, resulting in more height.[1][2]

Proponents point to the general fact that bone remodels in response to load. Medical sources describe the growth plate as the site where long bones lengthen, and note that growth plate injuries tend to impair growth.[3][4]
No clinical study has tested impact or microfracture for increasing height.

paras: Forum posts describe sprinting on asphalt, jumping on one leg with ankle weights, push presses and squats as ways to cause shin-bone microfractures, and posters report sensations they interpret as the bones being stressed.[1] A T Nation thread titled around stretching shin bones for height discusses microfractures as partial damage at bone junctions that osteoblasts fill in, as opposed to a complete break.[2]

sections.h: What medicine says about bone growth
paras: Wolff's law holds that bone adapts to the loads placed on it; loading strengthens bone, and examples include denser bones in the racquet arm of tennis players.[3] Longitudinal growth, however, occurs at cartilage growth plates near the ends of long bones. Plates fuse in adolescence, as early as 14 and most commonly 15 to 17 in boys, and in girls 14 to 15.[4]
Growth hormone drives chondrocyte division in the plate, and rising oestrogen in puberty slows it. Fractures involving the plate (Salter-Harris) tend to interfere with growth, height or function.[4]
High-impact loading can cause overuse injuries, and injury at the growth plate can impair growth rather than add to it.[4]

lore.intro: The idea circulates mainly among teenagers on looksmax.org and older bodybuilding forums.[1][2]

claims.claim: Microfractures in the leg bones trigger growth and add height.
Heavy loading adds bone, so loading legs adds length.
